A.explanation: A value of $10^{17}$ is about nine orders of magnitude too small and would imply an atomic volume far larger than $(10^{-10}\,\text{m})^3$.

B.explanation: Dividing a handset volume of about $10^{-4}\,\text{m}^3$ by an atomic volume of about $10^{-30}\,\text{m}^3$ gives about $10^{26}$ atoms.

C.explanation: A value of $10^{32}$ is too large and would require atoms much smaller than the known $10^{-10}\,\text{m}$ diameter.

D.explanation: A value of $10^{37}$ is far too large and would imply a sub-nuclear size for the volume of one atom.

hints: Estimate the handset volume from typical phone dimensions of about $0.15\,\text{m}$ by $0.07\,\text{m}$ by $0.01\,\text{m}$, which gives about $10^{-4}\,\text{m}^3$.
Treat one atom as a cube of side equal to the atomic diameter of about $10^{-10}\,\text{m}$, so its volume is about $(10^{-10}\,\text{m})^3$.
Divide the handset volume by the atomic volume using subtraction of powers of ten to get the order of magnitude of the number of atoms.
walkthrough: Estimate the handset volume: length $\approx 0.15\,\text{m}$, width $\approx 0.07\,\text{m}$ and thickness $\approx 0.01\,\text{m}$, so $V_{phone} \approx 0.15 \times 0.07 \times 0.01 \approx 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^3$.
Estimate the atomic volume: atomic diameter $\approx 10^{-10}\,\text{m}$, so modelling the atom as a cube gives $V_{atom} \approx (10^{-10}\,\text{m})^3 = 10^{-30}\,\text{m}^3$.
Use the suggested rule $N \approx V_{phone} / V_{atom}$ to count how many atomic volumes fit into the handset.
Substitute the orders of magnitude: $N \approx 10^{-4} / 10^{-30} = 10^{(-4+30)} = 10^{26}$, with no units as volume divided by volume.
This order of magnitude matches $10^{26}$ and is far from $10^{17}$, $10^{32}$ or $10^{37}$. This is option B.
